Cartesianism
kar-TEE-zhuh-niz-uhm
noun
The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650); from Cartesius, the Latin form of his name.

📖 Biblical Definition

Cartesianism is the philosophy that descends from René Descartes, the seventeenth-century French thinker who sought to rebuild all knowledge on a foundation of indubitable certainty, beginning by doubting everything that could be doubted until he reached the one thing he thought could not—cogito, ergo sum, “I think, therefore I am.” From the thinking self as the first certainty, Descartes proceeded to reason his way outward to God and the world. The dictionary recognizes Descartes’ brilliance and grants that he intended to defend, not destroy, belief in God. Yet Cartesianism set loose a method that has shaped the modern mind for the worse: it made the autonomous human reason, the doubting self, the foundation and judge of all knowledge, including the knowledge of God. Where Scripture begins with God—in the beginning God; the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge—Descartes begins with the self and reaches God only as a conclusion the self certifies. This inversion enthrones man’s mind as the measure and makes the Creator answerable to the bar of the creature’s reason. The Christian does not establish God by doubting; he knows God because God has spoken, and reasons from that revelation, leaning not unto his own understanding. The dictionary names Cartesian autonomy as a corruption of the right order of knowing, in which the fear of the LORD, not the doubting self, is the beginning.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The philosophy of Descartes founding knowledge on the doubting self (“I think, therefore I am”); named as the enthroning of autonomous reason against the biblical order that begins with God.

CARTESIANISM, the philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650).

Sought certainty by doubting all that could be doubted.

Founded knowledge on the thinking self: cogito, ergo sum.

Made autonomous human reason the foundation and judge of all knowledge.

Inverts the biblical order that begins with God, not the doubting self.

📖 Key Scripture

Pro 1:7 — "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction."

Pro 3:5 — "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding."

1Co 8:2 — "And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know."

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cartesianism founds knowledge on the autonomous doubting self and reaches God only as a conclusion; the biblical order begins with God and reasons from His revelation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the autonomy at the root of the Cartesian method: the making of the doubting human self the first certainty and the foundation of all knowledge, so that even God is reached only as a conclusion the mind certifies. This inverts the order Scripture lays down. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; in the beginning, God. To begin with the self and to make the Creator answerable to the bar of the creature’s reason is to enthrone man as the measure of all things—the very posture the apostle warns against, lest any be spoiled through philosophy after the rudiments of the world.

The principle to recover is the right order of knowing: God first, His revelation the foundation, the creature’s reason a servant under it. The Christian does not establish God by an act of doubt; he knows God because God has spoken, and he leans not unto his own understanding but trusts in the LORD with all his heart. Reason is good, and the Christian thinks rigorously; but he thinks as a creature under the Word, not as an autonomous judge above it. Whoever thinks he knows of himself knows nothing yet as he ought.
